1093.title: Victory as a funeral
1093.hook: weapons are tools of ill omen; mark even victory with mourning (Tao Te Ching 31)
1093.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-one as a call to use force only as a last resort and to grieve, not celebrate, what it costs, even in victory.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was where armies camp: wherever an army is stationed, briars and thorns spring up. Your line was no force.

Who mourns at a victory parade? Chapter thirty-one of the Tao Te Ching has an answer, and it's the general. Its instruction is about where people stand. At a ceremony, there's a side for celebrations and a side for funerals. And the chapter puts the winning commander on the funeral side, as if the victory itself were a burial. Strange advice for a winner. It's today's.
screen: `WHO MOURNS AT A VICTORY PARADE?` → `A SIDE FOR FEASTS, A SIDE FOR FUNERALS.` → `THE WINNER STANDS WITH THE MOURNERS.`

segments.voice: First, the weapons. In James Legge's translation the chapter opens: "Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen." However beautiful. A sword can be a lovely object, polished and balanced. The chapter doesn't deny it. It just won't let the beauty hide what the thing is for. Second, when they're used. The wise person reaches for weapons only when there's no other choice, and even then puts calm and restraint first. The chapter doesn't pretend force is never needed. It treats force as a last resort, picked up with reluctance. Third, no joy in winning. Whoever delights in killing people, the chapter says, won't get what they want in the world. Victory isn't to be called beautiful, because calling it beautiful means taking pleasure in the dead. Fourth, the funeral. The chapter says the left is the place of honor on festive occasions, and the right on occasions of mourning. Then it places the commanding general on the right. Those who have killed many, it says, should weep for them, and the victor takes his place as if at the rites of mourning. That's the title: victory as a funeral. Away from any battlefield, people still win things: an argument at dinner, a promotion someone else wanted, a point scored in front of a room. The chapter doesn't say lose on purpose. It says notice who's on the other side of your win, and don't dance on the field.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a disagreement you're likely to win; you have the facts. Now turn to the other person: what will they lose if you win loudly? Face, a little pride, the feeling of being heard. Look for one way to make your point and leave them standing: a softer word, a question instead of a verdict.
Victory as a funeral. Chapter thirty-one's instruction that even a won battle be marked the way mourners mark a death, with the general standing on the side of grief. Today's word.
Your line: win sadly. Someone is always on the other side of a win. Until tomorrow.

1094.title: Rivers to the sea
1094.hook: the Tao in the world is like rivers flowing to the sea (Tao Te Ching 32)
1094.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-two as a picture of influence without force: like the sea that streams flow into, the Tao draws things by being low and open rather than by pulling.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was victory as a funeral: even a won battle marked with grief. Your line was win sadly.

Rain hitting a roof doesn't decide where to go. It runs to the gutter, the gutter to the drain, the drain to a creek, the creek to a river. Nobody steers it. Nobody has to persuade a single drop. After two days of armies and weapons, chapter thirty-two of the Tao Te Ching turns to something much quieter: water going downhill, and dew settling on the ground. Its last line describes the Tao by the place where all the water ends up.
screen: `RAIN DOESN'T DECIDE WHERE TO GO.` → `NOBODY STEERS IT.` → `WHERE ALL THE WATER ENDS UP.`

segments.voice: First, the small thing nobody can master. The chapter opens by saying the Tao has no name. In its plain simplicity it may look small, and yet nobody in the world can make it a servant. Small is not the same as weak. Second, the dew. Heaven and earth come together, the chapter says, and send down sweet dew, and the dew reaches everywhere evenly, of its own accord, without anyone giving orders. No official decides which field gets watered. It just falls, and it falls on all of them. Third, names and stopping. Once things are shaped and divided, they get names, and once there are names, it's time to know where to stop. Legge's wording is that people can then know to rest in it, and so stay clear of failure. Some readers hear a warning in that: naming is useful, but endless sorting and labeling is where things go wrong. Fourth, the sea. The chapter closes, in James Legge's translation: "The relation of the Tao to all the world is like that of the great rivers and seas to the streams from the valleys." The streams aren't dragged to the sea. The sea doesn't chase them. They arrive because the sea is low and open, and water goes where it's received. It can be a picture of a person, too: the kitchen everyone drifts into at a party, the friend people call first. Not because they grabbed. Because there's room.

segments.voice: Find some water, at a window, a sink, a glass, or in your memory: a creek, a gutter in the rain. Watch it move; it never argues with the slope, it just takes the next low place, without hurrying and without stopping. Let your breath move at the same easy pace.
Rivers to the sea. Chapter thirty-two's closing picture: the Tao is to the world as the great rivers and seas are to the streams that run into them from the valleys. Today's word.
Your line: to the sea. Nobody has to drag a stream downhill. Same time tomorrow.

1095.title: Knowing yourself
1095.hook: knowing others is wisdom, knowing yourself is enlightenment; who knows they have enough is rich (Tao Te Ching 33)
1095.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often use chapter thirty-three as a prompt for self-examination: noticing their own reactions, mastering themselves rather than others, and learning to recognize enough.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was rivers to the sea: streams arrive at the low, open place without being pulled. Your line was to the sea.

A woman on a morning train watches the man across the aisle. Tight jaw, a glance at his phone, a sigh. In ten seconds she has a whole story about his day. An hour earlier she snapped at her brother over nothing, and that one came with a ready excuse attached, an excuse about him. Chapter thirty-three of the Tao Te Ching is short, and it's built in pairs: two kinds of knowing, two kinds of strength, two kinds of wealth. In each pair, one half points outward and the other points back at you.
screen: `A STRANGER'S FACE, OR YOUR OWN SNAP?` → `BUILT IN PAIRS.` → `ONE OUTWARD, ONE BACK AT YOU.`

segments.voice: First, knowing. In James Legge's translation the chapter opens: "He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent." Discerning is no small thing. Reading people is a real skill. But the chapter sets a second kind of knowing beside it, and the Chinese word there means bright, or clear. Seeing yourself is a kind of light. Second, strength. Whoever overcomes others is strong, the chapter says, and whoever overcomes themselves is mighty. Winning a fight takes muscle. Not starting the fight you were itching for takes something more. Third, wealth. You may remember this one from day thirteen of this path: whoever is content with what they have is rich. And whoever keeps going with steady effort, the chapter adds, has a firm will. It doesn't say stop trying. It holds enough and effort together. The rich person here isn't the one with the most; it's the one who can tell when there's enough. Fourth, the ending, which is a riddle. Whoever doesn't lose their place endures, it says, and whoever dies but doesn't perish has long life. Readers have heard different things in that line, and the chapter doesn't explain it. So, back on the train. The outward half of each pair is about other people: reading them, beating them, getting more than them. Chapter thirty-three keeps turning the mirror around. Knowing yourself, here, is catching the excuse before it finishes forming, and asking what in you just reacted.
screen: `KNOWING OTHERS, KNOWING YOURSELF.` · `STRONG, AND MIGHTY.` · `CONTENT, AND STEADY.` · `DYING, BUT NOT PERISHING.` · then, large: `HE WHO KNOWS HIMSELF IS INTELLIGENT.`

segments.voice: Go back over the last day and find one moment when you reacted: irritation, a quick yes you didn't mean, a sudden urge to leave. Don't judge it or explain it away; just ask quietly, what was that, in me? If an answer comes, keep it; if nothing does, the asking is enough.
Knowing yourself. Chapter thirty-three sets it beside knowing others: knowing others is discerning, and knowing yourself, it says, is clear and bright. Today's word.
Your line: know myself. The mirror turns back before it points out. See you tomorrow.

1096.title: Flowing everywhere
1096.hook: the great Tao flows everywhere and claims nothing (Tao Te Ching 34)
1096.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-four as a model for giving without seeking credit: doing the work, letting it spread, and not claiming the name for it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was knowing yourself: knowing others is discerning, and knowing yourself is clear. Your line was know myself.

The last slide of a group presentation is the one with everybody's names on it. Sometimes there's one person on it who quietly fixed the spreadsheet at midnight, rewrote the clumsy paragraph, and sent the reminder that got everyone there on time. Their name is on the slide in the same size font as everyone else's. They didn't ask for more. Chapter thirty-four of the Tao Te Ching describes the Tao a lot like that person: everywhere in the work, and nowhere on the credits.
screen: `THE SLIDE WITH EVERYONE'S NAMES.` → `THE ONE WHO FIXED IT AT MIDNIGHT.` → `EVERYWHERE IN THE WORK, NOWHERE ON THE CREDITS.`

segments.voice: First, the flood. In James Legge's translation the chapter begins: "All-pervading is the Great Tao! It may be found on the left hand and on the right." The Chinese word behind all-pervading has the sense of water overflowing, spilling in every direction at once. Not a channel. A flood plain. Second, no claim. The chapter says all things depend on it to come into being, and it doesn't turn any of them away. And when the work is done, it doesn't claim the name of having done it. It clothes and feeds everything, and doesn't set itself up as their master. Third, small and great at once. Because it asks for nothing, the chapter says, it can be called small. And because everything returns to it without even knowing it's there, it can be called great. The same thing, named both ways. Fourth, the sage. The chapter ends by saying the wise person does great things in the same way: by never trying to make himself great. Not hiding. Not pretending to be nothing. Just not reaching for the name. Credit is everywhere, at work, in families, online: a like, a thank-you, a name in the email. The chapter doesn't call wanting it wicked. It just describes something enormous that gives without keeping score, and suggests the wise do the same.

Flowing everywhere. Chapter thirty-four's great Tao, found on the left hand and the right, feeding everything and claiming none of it. Today's word.

1097.title: The bland Tao
1097.hook: music and fine food stop travelers, but the Tao is bland and never runs out (Tao Te Ching 35)
1097.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-five as an invitation to value plain, ordinary things, which seem dull beside entertainment and treats but do not run out.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was flowing everywhere: the great Tao feeding everything and claiming none of it. Your line was claim nothing.

Onions frying at a street fair. A band warming up by the food trucks. People who were walking somewhere else slow down, drift over, and stand there for a while with paper plates. An hour later they're gone, off to the next thing, and the band is packing up. Then, at home that night, somebody drinks a plain glass of water at the kitchen sink. Nobody photographs it. Nobody drifts over to watch. Chapter thirty-five of the Tao Te Ching sets those two scenes side by side, and it makes a surprising claim about which one lasts.
screen: `ONIONS AND A BAND AT A STREET FAIR.` → `A PLAIN GLASS OF WATER.` → `WHICH ONE LASTS?`

segments.voice: First, the great image. The chapter says that whoever holds the great image of the Tao, the whole world comes to them. And those who come find no harm there, only rest, peace and ease. Not excitement. Ease. Second, the street fair. In James Legge's translation: "Music and dainties will make the passing guest stop (for a time)." Dainties is an old word for treats. Notice the chapter doesn't condemn them. Music is good. Treats are good. They really do stop people. But the guest is passing, and the stop is for a time. Third, the bland part. The chapter says the Tao, when it's put into words, seems flat and has no flavor. Look at it, and it doesn't seem worth looking at. Listen, and it doesn't seem worth hearing. That's an odd thing for a book about the Tao to say about the Tao. It doesn't try to sell it. Fourth, the turn. After all that, the chapter's last words, in Legge's version: "the use of it is inexhaustible." The music ends. The plate gets empty. The plain thing never runs out. Back at the street fair, the chapter isn't against any of it: loud, salty, bright, gone by evening. It just sets the plain thing beside it. The chapter names no examples, but some readers think of the plain things nobody would post. Water. Sleep. A walk. The same friend, again.

Stay with something that has almost no flavor, and see how much is there anyway: coolness, weight, the breath after.
The bland Tao. Chapter thirty-five's claim that the Tao, put into words, seems flavorless and not worth a look, and yet its use never runs out. Today's word.

1098.title: Soft overcomes hard
1098.hook: the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong (Tao Te Ching 36)
1098.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-six's line that the soft overcomes the hard as a guide for conflict: meeting rigidity with patience and yielding rather than with more force.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the bland Tao: flavorless in words, and never running out. Your line was bland and endless.

A door slammed hard often bounces back open. The same door, pushed gently until it meets the frame, clicks and stays shut. A shouting match is the slammed-door version: the harder one side pushes, the harder it comes back. You met this idea early on this path, with the swimmer who moved with the falls. Chapter thirty-six of the Tao Te Ching puts it in one plain sentence, today's title. But it arrives after some puzzling lines, read in more than one way.
screen: `A SLAMMED DOOR BOUNCES BACK.` → `PUSHED GENTLY, IT CLICKS SHUT.` → `A PLAIN SENTENCE, A PUZZLING SETUP.`

segments.voice: First, the turning. The chapter opens with a run of reversals. What is going to shrink is first stretched out. What is going to be weakened is first made strong. What is going to fall is first raised up. What is going to be taken is first given. Legge calls this hiding the light. Second, the two readings. Some readers hear those lines as strategy: flatter your rival, let them overreach, then strike. Others hear them as a description of how things move on their own: a wave swells before it breaks, a career peaks before it fades, and whatever puffs itself up is already on the way down. The chapter doesn't settle it. Third, the sentence. In James Legge's translation: "The soft overcomes the hard; and the weak the strong." Whichever way the opening is read, this line points one way. The swollen, rigid thing is the one about to turn. The yielding thing is still there afterward. Fourth, the fish. The chapter ends by saying a fish shouldn't be taken out of the deep, and a state's sharp tools shouldn't be shown off to the people. A fish is safe where it's hidden, in deep water. Strength on display invites the very reversal the chapter began with. In a hard conversation, the hard response is the slammed door: the clipped reply, the raised voice, the shown teeth. The soft response isn't giving up. It's the door that meets the frame and stays shut.
screen: `STRETCHED BEFORE IT SHRINKS.` · `STRATEGY, OR HOW THINGS TURN?` · `THE SOFT OVERCOMES THE HARD.` · `THE FISH STAYS IN THE DEEP.` · then, large: `THE WEAK THE STRONG.`

segments.voice: Notice your shoulders, your jaw, your hands, and let whichever is tightest soften a little. Then bring to mind a hard edge you might meet today, a curt email, a stubborn kid, and rehearse once a soft answer: not a surrender, just the plain fact without the edge, and a pause before you speak.
Soft overcomes hard. Chapter thirty-six's plain sentence: the soft overcomes the hard, and the weak the strong. Today's word.
Your line: soft overcomes hard. The door that meets the frame gently is the one that stays shut. I'll be here tomorrow.

1099.title: Doing nothing, nothing undone
1099.hook: the Tao does nothing, yet nothing is left undone (Tao Te Ching 37)
1099.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-seven's 'doing nothing' as not forcing: setting things up well, then letting them unfold without constant interference.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was soft overcomes hard: the yielding outlasts the rigid. Your line was soft overcomes hard.

Bread dough, under a towel on the counter. All afternoon, nobody touches it. Nobody kneads, nobody checks, nobody helps. And when the towel comes off, it has swelled over the rim of the bowl. This week's chapters kept circling that kind of thing: the army whose thorns outlast its win, the victor who mourns, streams finding the sea, the mirror turned back on yourself, the flood that claims nothing, the plain taste, the soft door. Chapter thirty-seven gathers it into one sentence, and today's word is the first half of it.
screen: `DOUGH UNDER A TOWEL.` → `NOBODY TOUCHES IT. IT RISES.` → `A WEEK GATHERED INTO ONE SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence. In James Legge's translation: "The Tao in its regular course does nothing (for the sake of doing it), and so there is nothing which it does not do." Doing nothing there is wu wei, the word you met early on this path: acting without forcing. Look at Legge's parentheses. He's warning the reader: this isn't laziness. The Tao isn't asleep. It just doesn't do things for the sake of doing them, doesn't push, doesn't fuss. And somehow, nothing is left undone. Second, what follows. The chapter says if rulers could hold on to this, all things would transform by themselves. Not be transformed by a decree. Transform, on their own, the way dough rises. Third, when wanting stirs. The chapter admits that even in that quiet, desire starts to rise up again: the urge to step in, to improve, to manage. Its answer is to settle that urge with the nameless simplicity, the same uncarved plainness from chapter twenty-eight. Fourth, stillness. The chapter ends: without desire, there is stillness, and the world settles itself. Tradition treats this chapter as the close of the book's first part, the part about the Tao. Tomorrow the second part begins. In a household or an office, the opposite looks like the parent hovering over the homework, the manager rewriting every email, the gardener tugging seedlings to help them grow. Sometimes the useful thing is to set things up well and take your hands off. The bread doesn't need you watching it.
screen: `DOES NOTHING, AND NOTHING IS UNDONE.` · `THINGS TRANSFORM BY THEMSELVES.` · `SETTLE THE URGE WITH PLAINNESS.` · `STILLNESS, AND THE WORLD SETTLES.` · then, large: `NOTHING WHICH IT DOES NOT DO.`

segments.voice: Start with the breath: don't do it, let it happen, the in-breath coming without being called and the out-breath leaving without a push. Then think of one thing you've been hovering over, a project, a person, a plan. Picture it set on the counter under a towel, not abandoned, just left to rise on its own for a while.
Doing nothing. The first half of chapter thirty-seven's sentence: the Tao does nothing for the sake of doing it, and so there is nothing it does not do. Today's word.
Your line: nothing undone. Hands off isn't the same as giving up. That's the week.

chat.says: How can the Tao do nothing and still leave nothing undone?

It does a little each day, so the work slowly gets done in the end.
It means the Tao is asleep, so people must do everything in its place.
chat.meaning: Chapter thirty-seven: the Tao does nothing for the sake of doing it, and so there is nothing it does not do. Things transform by themselves.
